_about: Customer words for every message the server sends to a screen (UI standard, product owner 2026-10-16): a short label for the main screen and a structured detail — what it means, why, what to do next — for its pop-up. Read by core/messages.py; values fill {placeholders}.

detail.what: The request could not be completed.
detail.next: Try again. If it keeps happening, raise a request in Support and say when it happened.

detail.what: What you asked for does not exist, or your organisation cannot see it.
Your role does not include this action.
detail.next: Ask an administrator in your organisation.

detail.what: {what}
Temperature, rainfall and soil moisture for every place on land, from the Copernicus ERA5 and ERA5-Land reanalysis produced by ECMWF.
detail.why: The drought, heat, soil-water and frost scores are measured on it.

detail.what: Monthly rainfall, temperature and evaporation over each crop's growing areas worldwide, from Copernicus ERA5-Land.
detail.why: It tests how closely each crop's harvest has followed the weather in past seasons.

detail.what: Production, area and yield by country and region, from FAOSTAT, Eurostat, the US Department of Agriculture and Statistics Canada.
detail.why: They show how far each crop's harvest fell in past bad years. That sets how a hazard score becomes lost volume, and a euro figure is published only where this test passes.

detail.what: Annual forest loss worldwide, from Hansen Global Forest Change (University of Maryland).
detail.why: It is read for each plot when a deforestation check under the EU Deforestation Regulation runs.

detail.what: Monthly prices from the World Bank commodity price data (the Pink Sheet) and the European Commission's agri-food data portal.
detail.why: They show the input-cost pressure that observed price moves put on your sourcing spend.

detail.what: Price pressure is measured on the spend of your sourcing plots, and none are on file.
detail.next: Add your plots under Suppliers & crops.

detail.what: No price series is loaded for {commodity}, so its spend carries no price move.
detail.next: Load a price series for it with Load indices.

detail.what: The price series for {commodity} does not say which currency it is quoted in, so its move cannot be measured in {currency}.
detail.next: Load the series again with the currency it is quoted in.

detail.what: There is no {quote} to {currency} exchange rate for {period}, so the price move for {commodity} cannot be measured in {currency}.

agri.data.price.row_value.label: Index value is not a number

detail.what: Each row needs its index value as a number.
Each row needs the commodity and the month, written as year and month (for example 2026-09).
Each row needs the currency its price is quoted in, as a three-letter code (for example USD).
{currency} is not a currency the platform can convert. Use a three-letter currency code (for example USD or EUR).

agri.data.price.no_rows.label: No usable rows in the file

detail.what: None of the rows could be used. The first problem is in row {row}: {reason}.
detail.next: Download the template, fill in its columns and load the file again.

detail.what: Upload the days past due of your agricultural loans. Each past-due loan is then sorted into harvest carry-over, a bad harvest, or genuine deterioration.
detail.next: Choose the currency and book date, then upload the file.

detail.what: {days} days past due in {month}, inside the harvest window for {crop} and within the {cap}-day seasonal limit.
detail.why: Farm income arrives after the harvest, so arrears in this window are usually repaid from the next sale.

detail.what: National {crop} production in {country} fell {fall}% on the year before, in the {season} season. The loan is {days} days past due.
detail.why: A national bad harvest explains a pattern. It does not prove that this borrower's own harvest failed.

detail.what: {days} days past due is beyond the {cap}-day seasonal limit, so the harvest cycle does not explain it.
{month} is outside the harvest window for {crop}, so harvest carry-over does not explain this arrear.

agri.data.arrears.no_calendar.label: No harvest calendar for this crop

detail.what: There is no harvest calendar for {crop}, so the loan gets no seasonal allowance.
The loan has no crop on record, so no harvest window applies and it gets no seasonal allowance.
detail.next: Add the crop the loan finances to the upload.

agri.data.arrears.no_country.label: No country, so no harvest check

detail.what: The loan has no country on record, so national harvest figures could not be checked. It is counted as genuine.
detail.next: Add the borrower's country (a two-letter code) to the upload.

agri.data.arrears.row_days.label: Days past due is not a whole number

detail.what: Each row needs its days past due as a whole number.
Each row needs the loan's reference.

agri.data.arrears.no_rows.label: No usable rows in the file

detail.what: None of the rows could be used. The first problem is in row {row}: {reason}.
detail.next: Download the template, fill in its columns and upload the file again.

agri.data.file_unreadable.label: The file could not be read

detail.what: The file is not a readable CSV file.
detail.next: Save it as CSV (comma-separated values) and try again.

detail.what: The file holds no rows to use, at most a header line.
detail.next: Download the template, fill in its columns and try again.

detail.what: Passed a test against observed outcomes it was not built from. Its scores may lead a headline and carry a figure.
A published, authoritative layer used to screen. It is not validated, so it never leads a headline and never carries a figure. Where it was tested, the result is in its details.
A projection of the future, a climate statistic or an observation: there is nothing observed to test it against. Context only; it never leads a headline.
A map of zones or an inventory: where a hazard is, with no climate projection.
A hazard on our plan that is not covered yet.
It was tested against an independent observed record and did not reach the bar to be validated. The result is under How it was tested.
No observed record to test it against has been found at scale yet.
Validated in at least {min} of the {n} world regions, including at least one of Latin America and the Caribbean, Africa or Asia.
Validated on a sample spread across the world. Results for each region are not reported yet, so no region is shown as validated on its own.
Validated in two or more world regions, or in one with mixed results in others. Not a worldwide claim.
Validated in a single world region. Elsewhere it is untested or does not hold.
No world region is validated yet.

coverage.hazard.heat_wave.label: ERA5 climate reanalysis, crop heat scale

detail.what: How hot a place runs for crops: where its temperature sits in the crop's heat-stress band, and how unusually hot the year is against the 1991–2020 normal. Read from the ERA5 climate reanalysis.
detail.why: Checked against observed cocoa production in West Africa (FAO and ICCO), a record independent of the climate data: over 34 years, rank agreement 0.60.
detail.next: Validated for cocoa only. Bordeaux wine grapes showed no heat signal (0.01). A crop heat-stress scale, not a measure of heat damage to buildings.

detail.what: The number of days a year above 30 °C, counted from 30 years of daily maximum temperatures (NASA POWER).
detail.why: Checked against hot days counted at 248 weather stations in Europe and the United States (NOAA GHCN-Daily, 1991–2020), which the data source does not use: rank agreement 0.92.
detail.next: Africa has no weather station with enough complete years to test, and Latin America has 3, so neither is validated. Stations sit mostly at airports. It counts hot days; it is not a damage estimate.

detail.what: Two scores. Cold wave: how far the 1-in-10-year coldest night falls below the point where pipes freeze and below the cold a building was designed for, from 30 years of daily minimum temperatures (NASA POWER). Frost: the coldest night of the coldest month, on a crop scale.
detail.why: The cold-wave score was checked against the coldest nights at 248 weather stations in Europe and the United States (NOAA GHCN-Daily, 1991–2020): rank agreement 0.89.
detail.next: The frost score is a crop scale and is not used as a building hazard. Africa has no weather station with enough complete years to test, and Latin America has 3, so neither is validated. Stations sit mostly at airports.

coverage.hazard.wildfire.label: Copernicus fire weather and satellite burn history

detail.what: How often fire weather reaches extreme danger (Copernicus Fire Weather Index, 2006–2020), weighted by the share of land that can burn, plus the burn history seen by satellite (ESA Climate Change Initiative, 2001–2019). A fixed, published formula.
detail.why: Checked on the official European burn record (EFFIS, 41,000 burn scars) for 2022–2024, later than every input: it finds burned places with a hit rate of 0.76 and ranks burned area with rank agreement 0.37, just above the {bar} bar. Gridded burned-area records also pass in Africa, Asia, Latin America and Oceania.
detail.next: Most of the skill comes from past burn history, which overlaps the test record; fire weather and fuel alone reach 0.68 and 0.22. In North America gridded burned area passes but fire-perimeter records fall just short. A same-day fire-weather version did not pass (0.44) and is not used.

detail.what: How much a place warms under a climate scenario, against today's climate, from the average of the CMIP6 climate models.
detail.why: It is a projection of the future, so there is no observed outcome to test it against.
detail.next: Shown only under a future scenario and year; it has no value for today. Context only: it never leads a headline.

detail.what: How far apart the warmest and coldest months lie, and how much the year-to-year values spread, from the 1991–2020 monthly climate normals.
detail.why: It describes the climate rather than a damage, so testing it against weather stations would prove nothing.
detail.next: Context only: it never leads a headline.

detail.what: The probability that the ground at a place is permafrost, from the published 1 km northern-hemisphere permafrost map (Obu et al., 2019).
detail.why: Checked against ground temperatures measured in 229 boreholes of the Global Terrestrial Network for Permafrost, never used to build the map: rank agreement 0.82, well above the {bar} bar.
detail.next: Northern hemisphere only, from 25° north; Central Asia and Tibet have 12 boreholes, too few to judge. It shows where permafrost is, not the damage from its thaw.

detail.what: The 1-in-10-year wind speed at a place from tropical cyclones, modelled from every storm track recorded since 1981 in IBTrACS, the international best-track archive.
detail.why: Rebuilt from the storm seasons before a test window and checked on the storms that came after: rank agreement 0.78 to 0.88 across five windows of at least 10 seasons.
detail.next: A test of wind strength, not of damage: observed wind damage and insured losses are not tested yet. The score and the test come from the same track archive, split in time. Europe's sample is thin (30 places).

detail.what: How strong the yearly peak wind gusts are at a place, from the ERA5 climate reanalysis: the European winter windstorms, blizzards and dust storms that tropical-cyclone models miss.
detail.why: Checked against peak gusts measured at 92 weather stations (NOAA): rank agreement 0.57 overall, 0.79 in Europe (34 stations) and 0.38 in North America (58 stations, a narrow pass).
detail.next: It ranks places by gust hazard; it is not a loss model. Against NOAA's reported gusts it reaches 0.26, and against US damaging-event counts 0.05, so no euro figure is published for it.

detail.what: How much near-surface wind speed changes at a place under a climate scenario, from the average of the CMIP6 climate models. A rise and a fall both count.
detail.why: It is a projection of the future, so there is no observed outcome to test it against.
detail.next: Shown only under a future scenario and year. Context only: it never leads a headline.

coverage.hazard.tornado.label: ERA5 storm instability and wind shear

detail.what: How often the air above a place has the instability and wind shear that breed tornadoes, large hail and damaging winds, from a published severe-storm index (Taszarek, 2021) on the ERA5 climate reanalysis.
detail.why: Checked against 70,000 tornadoes recorded by NOAA's Storm Prediction Center: it finds them with a hit rate of 0.73 (0.74 for the stronger ones). Rebuilt from earlier years, it reaches 0.82 on later ones.
detail.next: It describes the storm environment, not damage: it does not rank US counties by reported damage (0.09).

detail.what: How much drier than normal a place is, from the SPEI drought index: rainfall set against the water that evaporation takes.
detail.why: Checked against observed crop-production shocks (FAO) over 34 years in 21 crop regions. It holds for rain-fed winter cereals and tree crops in dry climates: Australian wheat (0.64), North African wheat (0.47 to 0.67), West and Central Asian wheat (0.40 to 0.57) and central Spain (0.56).
detail.next: Not a general drought score: it does not hold for humid, irrigated or summer crops, such as the US Corn Belt, Brazil, Argentina, Indian rice and cane, Nigeria and South Africa.

detail.what: The share of a place inside the 1-in-100-year river floodplain, and the damage expected at its average flood depth, from the JRC global river-flood maps (Copernicus Emergency Management Service, 90 m, seven return periods).
detail.why: Checked on the flood extents Copernicus mapped in six floods from 2019 to 2024, none of which the maps were built from: rank agreement 0.68 across 144 mapped places, hit rate 0.80. River floods are found well (hit rate 0.77 to 0.85); the Ahr flash flood was not (0.28).
detail.next: River flooding only: surface-water, flash and groundwater floods are not covered, and coastal flooding is its own hazard. The maps assume no flood defences. It does not rank US places by flood-insurance claims (0.08): a hazard score, not a loss model.

detail.what: How dry the soil around plant roots normally is at a place, compared with other land, from the ERA5-Land climate reanalysis.
detail.why: Checked against the loss of water stored on land seen by NASA's GRACE satellites from 2002 to 2026, at 3,124 places: rank agreement 0.08, so it stays an indicator.
detail.next: Observed water loss is driven by groundwater pumping, reservoirs and snow, which a soil-dryness score does not model.

coverage.hazard.sea_level_rise.label: Tide gauges and IPCC sea-level rise

detail.what: How high a site stands above the 1-in-10-year extreme sea level observed at the nearest tide gauge (GESLA-3, 1,864 gauges, 1979–2020), with the sea-level rise the IPCC Sixth Assessment projects and its likely range.
detail.why: The extreme level rebuilt from gauge years up to 2010 ranks the peaks the same gauges recorded from 2011 to 2020 with rank agreement 0.92 (810 gauges). At US gauges, the score ranks the peaks observed from 2014 to 2023 at 0.41 (218 gauges).
detail.next: A test of extreme still-water levels, not of flood depth or damage. Sites with no gauge within 250 km are not scored. The gauge network is densest in Europe and North America.

detail.what: How much rain falls in a place's wettest month, and how much that month varies from year to year, from the 1991–2020 monthly climate normals.
detail.why: Checked against the largest one-day rainfall of each year at 248 weather stations (NOAA GHCN-Daily): rank agreement 0.69, with 0.70 in the United States and 0.42 in Europe.
detail.next: Africa has no weather station with enough complete years to test, and Latin America has 3, so neither is validated. Stations sit mostly at airports.

coverage.hazard.saline_intrusion.label: Coastal elevation and IPCC sea-level rise

detail.what: How low and how close to the coast a place lies, raised by the sea-level rise the IPCC projects.
detail.why: Checked against the salinity measured in coastal groundwater at 3,400 monitoring points (Thorslund and van Vliet, 2020): rank agreement 0.10, so it stays an indicator.
detail.next: Real salinity depends on the rock, on pumping and on the nearest source of salt water, which elevation and distance to the coast do not capture.

detail.what: How much a place's rainfall changes under a climate scenario, from the average of the CMIP6 climate models. Drying and wetting both count.
detail.why: It is a projection of the future, so there is no observed outcome to test it against.
detail.next: Shown only under a future scenario and year. Context only: it never leads a headline.

detail.what: How unevenly rain falls through the year, and how much it varies from year to year, from the 1991–2020 monthly climate normals.
detail.why: It describes the climate rather than a damage, so testing it would prove nothing.
detail.next: Context only: it never leads a headline.

detail.what: How acidic the surface ocean is near a coastal or marine site, from the OceanSODA-ETHZ global record of ocean pH.
detail.why: It is already an observation, so there is nothing separate to test it against.
detail.next: For aquaculture, fisheries and other marine exposure only; it does not apply to inland sites or to buildings.

detail.what: Whether a site lies within reach of a mapped glacial lake, scaled by the lake's size, from a global inventory of 117,000 glacial lakes (GIGLak).
detail.why: Outbursts happen at the mapped lakes themselves, so a test of nearness against past outbursts would be circular. It is a reference layer, like volcano and earthquake zones.
detail.next: A nearness screen, not a model of where flood water flows: it includes places near a lake but not downstream of it.

detail.what: How prone the ground at a place is to landslides, from slope and geology, using NASA's global landslide susceptibility map (LHASA).
detail.why: Checked against 9,500 landslides in NASA's Global Landslide Catalog: hit rate 0.95, and places rated high or above see 11 times more landslides.
detail.next: NASA used the same catalogue to develop the map, so this repeats the map's published accuracy rather than a fresh test.

detail.what: How fast the ground is sinking, measured by satellite radar (Copernicus European Ground Motion Service, 2020–2024, 100 m), on a scale of 0 to 20 mm a year. Outside its coverage a published susceptibility class (Herrera, 2021) is shown as an indicator.
detail.why: The sinking rate fitted on 2020–2021 ranks the rate the same 200,000 places showed in 2022–2024 with rank agreement 0.85.
detail.next: Measured ground motion exists for Europe only. Elsewhere the susceptibility class stays an indicator (0.21 and 0.10 in tests) and never leads a headline. A test of measured motion, not of damage.

detail.what: How far the shoreline is projected to retreat at a place under each scenario and year (JRC, Vousdoukas et al., 2020).
detail.why: Checked against the shoreline change seen by satellite from 1984 to 2016 at 11,252 places on 67 coasts: the 2050 score ranks observed erosion at 0.36.
detail.next: The projection was built partly from the same shoreline trends, so this shows consistency rather than independent skill; it stays an indicator.

detail.what: How much soil water erosion moves off cropland each year, in tonnes per hectare, from the GloSEM global model (about 100 m).
detail.why: Checked against sediment measured in 204 European river catchments (0.09) and 670 reservoirs worldwide (0.08). Allowing for how much eroded soil reaches the outlet moves these only to 0.11 and 0.12, so it stays an indicator.
detail.next: The model gives erosion at a point, while the measurements cover whole catchments.

detail.what: Whether land is degraded under the UN Sustainable Development Goal indicator 15.3.1 (land cover, productivity and soil carbon), read from the Trends.Earth map.
detail.why: Checked against an independent 30 m land-productivity map (Li et al., 2025) at 4,000 points around the Mediterranean: rank agreement −0.17, the wrong direction, so it stays an indicator.
detail.next: Tested on two Mediterranean areas only.

coverage.hazard.avalanche.label: Terrain slope and a snow-climate estimate

detail.what: Whether slopes at a place are steep enough for avalanches to start, weighted by an estimate of snow climate from elevation and latitude.
detail.why: Checked against 4,367 avalanche start zones recorded in the Swiss Alps (SLF, 1970/71 to 2023/24): hit rate 0.67, rank agreement 0.29. Within high alpine terrain, from 1,500 m, the hit rate is 0.52, no better than chance.
detail.next: It separates mountains from lowlands and nothing more. Tested in Switzerland only.

detail.what: Whether a place has both permafrost (Obu et al., 2019) and the gentle slopes on which frozen, waterlogged soil creeps downhill.
detail.why: No observed record of soil creep exists at scale to test it against yet.
detail.next: A susceptibility flag, not a model of movement. It applies only where there is permafrost.

detail.what: The shaking a place has felt from recorded earthquakes, estimated from their size and distance (USGS and EMSC catalogues, with the Bakun–Wentworth intensity relation).
detail.why: A consistency check only (rank agreement 0.81 near the source, hit rate 0.96): the score is built from the same catalogue it is checked against. An independent test is pending.
detail.next: Earthquakes do not respond to climate; the score is the same in every scenario.

detail.what: How exposed a place is to a volcano's near-vent hazards and ash fall, from the Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program catalogue: about 1,200 volcanoes and the size of their recorded eruptions.
detail.why: Eruptions are too rare for a test at the level of a single place, so it stays an indicator.
detail.next: Hazard zones are circles around the volcano, with no wind or terrain. Where the catalogue records no eruption size, a moderate one (VEI 3) is assumed. No euro figure is published for it.

coverage.hazard.pollution.label: Air quality against WHO guideline levels

detail.what: How far air pollution exceeds the World Health Organization's 2021 air-quality guideline levels.
detail.why: No observed outcome record to test it against has been set up yet.
detail.next: Its coverage is limited.

detail.what: Over 34 years, rank agreement 0.60 with observed cocoa production. Cocoa only.

coverage.region.heat_wave.europe.label: No signal in Bordeaux wine harvests

detail.what: Over 34 years, rank agreement 0.01 with wine-grape yields: no heat signal.
Rank agreement 0.85 with the hot days counted at 115 weather stations.
Rank agreement 0.91 with the hot days counted at 133 weather stations.
Rank agreement 0.93 with the days above 30 °C at 48 weather stations.
Rank agreement 0.73 at 114 weather stations, mostly in Australia.
The cold-wave score: rank agreement 0.89 with the coldest nights at 115 weather stations.
The cold-wave score: rank agreement 0.86 at 133 weather stations.
Rank agreement 0.82 with the 1-in-10-year coldest night at 48 weather stations. Oceania has too little variation to judge.
On the 2022–2024 EFFIS record, hit rate 0.76 and rank agreement 0.37; on gridded burned area (GFED5), 0.76 across 5,853 places.
Burned area in 2021–2022, held out: rank agreement 0.67 (GFED5) and 0.77 (FireCCI) across 7,045 places.
Rank agreement 0.48 (GFED5) and 0.43 (FireCCI) across 19,045 places.
Rank agreement 0.53 (GFED5) and 0.57 (FireCCI) across 7,146 places.
Rank agreement 0.42 (GFED5) and 0.54 (FireCCI) across 3,126 places.

Rank agreement 0.64 with Australian wheat production over 34 years.

coverage.region.drought.europe.label: Central Spain and olives, not sugar beet

detail.what: Holds for central Spain (0.56) and olives (0.36); not for sugar beet (−0.27).
Holds for wheat in Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia (0.47 to 0.67); not for sorghum in Nigeria (0.18) or maize in South Africa (0.15).

coverage.region.drought.asia.label: West and Central Asian wheat holds

detail.what: Holds for wheat in Iran, Kazakhstan, Syria and Turkey (0.40 to 0.57); not for rice (0.19) or sugar cane (−0.01) in India.

coverage.region.drought.north_america.label: Corn Belt and prairies do not hold

detail.what: US Corn Belt −0.06; Canadian prairies 0.22.

coverage.region.drought.latin_america_ca.label: Argentina and Brazil do not hold

detail.what: Argentine wheat 0.09; Brazilian coffee −0.43 and soy −0.22.
Six observed floods, 2019–2024: rank agreement 0.68 and hit rate 0.80 at 144 mapped places. The coarser global flood record does not hold here (0.285 at 800 places).

coverage.region.flood.latin_america_cari.label: Global flood record holds on rank

detail.what: Global Flood Database, 2000–2018: rank agreement 0.41 and hit rate 0.77 at 800 places.
Global Flood Database: rank agreement 0.354 and hit rate 0.82 at 800 places.
Global Flood Database: rank agreement 0.33 at 800 places, just under the {bar} bar.
Global Flood Database: hit rate 0.78 but rank agreement 0.31 at 800 places.
Global Flood Database: rank agreement 0.25 at 800 places.
The score ranks the peaks observed at 218 NOAA tide gauges with rank agreement 0.41.
Rank agreement 0.42 at 115 weather stations.
Rank agreement 0.70 at 133 weather stations.
Rank agreement 0.88 with the yearly largest one-day rainfall at 48 weather stations.
Rank agreement 0.84 at 114 weather stations, mostly in Australia.
Measured sinking, held out in time: rank agreement 0.85 across 200,000 places.
The susceptibility class reaches 0.22 at 4,834 places: an indicator only.
Storm seasons from 2003, held out: rank agreement 0.74 at 748 places.
Rank agreement 0.56 at 642 places.
Rank agreement 0.62 at 445 places, and 0.77 at 5,973 places for the stored score.
Rank agreement 0.75 at 268 places.
Rank agreement 0.53 at 229 places.
Rank agreement 0.70 at 30 places; Europe mostly sees the remnants of tropical storms.
Rank agreement 0.79 with the measured peak gusts at 34 stations. There are no stations in Germany, the Netherlands or Denmark.
Rank agreement 0.38 at 58 stations; against NOAA's reported gusts 0.26, under the bar.

coverage.region.permafrost_thaw.europe.label: Boreholes in Europe and the Arctic

detail.what: Rank agreement 0.82 across all 229 boreholes, and 0.58 at the 38 in Europe and the Arctic Atlantic.
Rank agreement 0.76 at 30 boreholes in the United States and Canada.
Rank agreement 0.85 at 190 boreholes in Russia and Siberia. Tibet has 12, too few to judge.
Each place's own warming and rainfall change from the CMIP6 climate models, with the spread across models carried as a band.
Each place's warming from the CMIP6 climate models changes the storm environment, with the spread across models as a band. How often storms occur, and how large they are, is not projected.

coverage.mode.sea_level_band.label: IPCC sea-level rise, with its likely range

detail.what: The sea-level rise the IPCC Sixth Assessment projects for each scenario and year, with its likely range carried as a band.
The score is the projected change itself, so it only has meaning under a future scenario.

coverage.mode.parametric_cc.label: Heavier rain for each degree of warming

detail.what: Extreme rainfall grows by a fixed share for each degree of warming in the scenario.

coverage.mode.parametric_warming.label: A stated shift for each degree

detail.what: The score moves by a stated amount for each degree of warming in the scenario.
Warming raises the coldest nights, so the score falls by a stated amount for each degree of warming.

coverage.mode.variability.label: Swings widen as the climate warms

detail.what: Year-to-year variability widens by a stated amount for each degree of warming.

coverage.mode.susceptibility_flat.label: Today's state, held in every scenario

detail.what: A map of the ground or of today's climate: a predisposition, not a forecast. It is the same in every scenario, by design.
Earthquakes and volcanoes do not respond to climate: the score is the same in every scenario, by design.
River-flood hazard rises with extreme rainfall, which intensifies by about {rate} for each degree of local warming, from each place's warming in the CMIP6 climate models.
detail.why: Clausius–Clapeyron scaling of extreme rainfall (IPCC Sixth Assessment, Working Group I, chapter 11).
detail.next: Changes in average rainfall and coastal flooding are left out; they are separate mechanisms.

detail.what: Tropical-cyclone strength rises about {rate} for each degree of local warming. The severity is scaled; the number of storms is not.
detail.why: IPCC Sixth Assessment, Working Group I, chapter 11: peak intensity, and the share of the strongest storms, rise with warming.

detail.what: The peak-gust climate is today's exposure and does not change by scenario here.
detail.why: ERA5 climate reanalysis, 10 m wind gusts, 1991–2020.

detail.what: Fire weather worsens about {rate} for each degree of local warming, plus a term for drying, from the CMIP6 climate models.
detail.why: IPCC Sixth Assessment, Working Group I, chapters 11 and 12.

detail.what: A site's height above extreme sea level shrinks as the sea rises, using the IPCC sea-level rise and its likely range, plus the regional term from ocean currents and heat.
detail.why: IPCC Sixth Assessment, Working Group I, chapter 9: sea-level rise against 1995–2014.
detail.next: Two smaller regional terms, and the sinking of the land where no measured rate exists, are follow-ons; see Model limitations.

detail.what: The wettest month's rainfall intensifies by about {rate} for each degree of warming in the scenario.
detail.why: Clausius–Clapeyron scaling (IPCC Sixth Assessment, Working Group I, chapter 11).

coverage.projection.cold_wave.label: Fewer damaging cold waves as it warms

detail.what: Warming raises the 1-in-10-year coldest night, so fewer cold waves reach the cold that damages buildings.
detail.why: IPCC Sixth Assessment, Working Group I, chapter 11: cold extremes decline with warming. NASA POWER daily minimum temperatures, 1991–2020.

detail.what: Warming raises the coldest night, so frost becomes less frequent.
detail.why: IPCC Sixth Assessment, Working Group I, chapter 11: frost days decline with warming.

detail.what: How often heat reaches the crop stress level rises with the scenario's warming, by a stated amount per degree.
detail.why: The warming of each NGFS scenario, applied per degree.

detail.what: The number of hot days rises with the scenario's warming, by a stated amount per degree.
detail.why: The warming of each NGFS scenario, applied per degree.

coverage.projection.drought.label: Drier for each degree of warming

detail.what: Warming raises evaporation, so drought rises by a stated drying amount for each degree.
detail.why: The warming of each NGFS scenario, applied per degree.

coverage.projection.soil_water.label: Root zone drier for each degree

detail.what: Warming dries the root zone, through more evaporation and less snow carried over, by a stated amount per degree.

detail.what: Warming from the CMIP6 climate models raises the instability of the air by about {low} to {high} per degree, which moves the storm index by its square root, with wind shear held at today's level. It is read through the same NOAA tornado record the score is tested on.
detail.why: Romps (2016); IPCC Sixth Assessment, Working Group I, sections 11.7.3.5 and 12.4.5.3: instability rises with high confidence, and Europe is more likely than not to see more frequent severe-storm environments.
detail.next: Not projected: how often hail, tornadoes and damaging winds occur, beyond what the changed environment implies; the size of hailstones; wind shear and the air's resistance to storms, held at today's level. Places already at the top of the scale cannot rise further.

coverage.limitation.water_management.label: Irrigation does not explain yields better than rain

detail.what: Water stress is scored from rainfall-based drought and soil moisture, not from the reservoirs farmers irrigate from. We tested whether stored basin water explains an irrigated crop's yield better than rainfall does; it does not.
detail.why: On Spanish river basins, each year left out in turn: stored water explained none of the change in sugar-beet yields in the Duero (−0.12, with the wrong sign: fuller reservoirs, lower yields), nor of rice in the Guadalquivir (0.00). Re-tested twice, with the same result.
detail.next: A water-management record (basin allocations, canal deliveries or a global irrigation dataset) that explains at least {r2} of yields on years it was not fitted to, over the same years as the drought score.

coverage.limitation.water_management.tod.label: Irrigated plots shown as an upper bound

detail.what: An irrigated plot's drought score is shown as an upper bound, and its euro figure is left unchanged. No buffer is invented.

coverage.limitation.regional_sea_level.label: Regional sea-level rise is partly applied

detail.what: Coastal flood projections use the IPCC global-mean sea-level rise plus its largest regional term, from ocean currents and heat, so local sea level differs from the global mean. Two smaller regional terms, the pull of melting ice sheets and the slow rebound of land after the ice age, are not applied place by place yet.
detail.why: With the ocean term, the US East coast and north-west Europe read about 0.1 m above the global mean, as the IPCC Sixth Assessment documents there.
detail.next: The full IPCC regional sea-level dataset (about 9 GB, which also carries land motion) for the two remaining terms.

coverage.limitation.regional_sea_level.t.label: Global mean used for the remaining terms

detail.what: The ocean term is applied and disclosed; the two other terms use the global-mean rise until the full dataset is read in.

coverage.limitation.land_subsidence.label: Coastal land sinking needs a measured rate

detail.what: Coastal exposure is sea-level rise plus the local sinking of the land. In several large deltas, such as Jakarta, the US Gulf coast and parts of the North Sea coast, the land sinks faster than the sea rises. The coastal height check subtracts each place's sinking up to the year shown, where a measured rate exists.
detail.why: The coastal score subtracts the sinking rate times the years to the horizon. No rate has been loaded yet, so the term counts as zero.
detail.next: Copernicus European Ground Motion Service rates for EU coasts, or a global satellite land-motion product.

coverage.limitation.land_subsidence.toda.label: No rate yet, so sinking counts as zero

detail.what: The model handles sinking; with no rate the term is zero, which understates exposure where the land sinks. Disclosed, never assumed.

coverage.limitation.financial_euro_basis.label: Financial euros rest on your stated method

detail.what: The agricultural crop euro figure is validated: a regression on observed yields that must explain at least {r2} on years it was not fitted to. Hazard scores are validated for ranking places only, and every test against observed losses failed. So financial euro figures (haircut, damage ratio, event frequency, loadings) are computed only from the values your institution states for the year and a second person attests. The platform supplies none.
detail.why: Every money figure is checked against the register of stated values, and a number in a money calculation that is not registered is refused.
detail.next: An observed loss record for each peril, for example realised loss rates by hazard, that would let a platform damage model pass a test against losses, as the crop models do. Until then, your institution's method is the basis.

coverage.limitation.financial_euro_basis.label: A value not stated leaves the figure missing

detail.what: Every money figure records the stated values it used. A value not stated leaves the figure missing, and a filing with a missing figure cannot be submitted.

coverage.limitation.flood_mechanism_scop.label: Flood projection scales extreme rainfall only

detail.what: The forward flood projection scales the hazard by how much heavier extreme rainfall becomes with warming, about 7% per °C. Changes in average rainfall, and coastal or combined flooding, are left out on purpose: they are separate mechanisms.
detail.why: IPCC Sixth Assessment, Working Group I, chapter 11.
detail.next: Add the average-rainfall term and the combined coastal and surface-water effect, each cited and with a band.

coverage.limitation.flood_mechanism_scop.label: Extreme-rainfall scaling, with a model band

detail.what: Extreme rainfall is the main flood driver, and it is applied with a real band across the CMIP6 climate models.

solvency.missing.premiums_outside.label: {peril}: premiums for other countries not stated

detail.what: You insure {peril_lower} risks in countries outside the EU, Andorra, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Monaco, Norway, San Marino, Switzerland and the Vatican. The standard formula charges them on the premiums you earn there, region by region. Those premiums are not stated, so these risks carry no {peril_lower} charge yet.
detail.why: Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/35 charges risks outside the countries of its Annex XIII on premiums (Articles 121(8) to 124(9)), and template S.27.01.01 reports those premiums by the regions of Annex III. The charge is never computed on a premium of zero.
detail.next: State the premiums for each region under Your data → Add and provide data (Solvency II) and have them attested.

detail.what: Each risk is placed in its zone from its postal code (Annex IX), weighted by the zone's risk weight (Annex X) and combined with the zone correlations (Annexes XXII to XXVI).

solvency.incurred.comparison.label: Actual and modelled figures do not reconcile

detail.what: Incurred losses are actual claims for a past period (IFRS S2 paragraph 16(a)). The expected yearly loss, the modelled 1-in-200 loss and the standard-formula capital look forward (paragraph 16(c) and (d)).
detail.why: A model gives the whole range of possible years; a period's claims are one year that happened. The two do not add up or reconcile.
detail.next: Follow them side by side over the years: that shows how well the models track what happens.

Places scored higher recorded more {events}: the ranking agreement between score and count is {rho}, and the count rises from one score band to the next.
detail.why: A score that orders places the way the observed record does is faithful to that record.

detail.what: The ranking agreement between the score and the count of {events} is {rho}, but the count does not rise from one score band to the next.
The ranking agreement between the score and the count of {events} is {rho}, below the {floor} this check requires.
The scores or the counts of {events} barely vary, so their ranking agreement cannot be measured.

validation.record.no_catalogue.label: No event record for this hazard

detail.what: This check runs only for the hazards whose observed event catalogue the platform holds: earthquakes and tropical cyclones.

validation.record.no_data.label: No scores or events on file

detail.what: No current scores or no observed events are on file for this hazard, so the check cannot run.
detail.next: It runs once both are loaded.

portfolio.forward.basis.label: Highest hazard score against your at-risk level

detail.what: An asset counts as at risk when its highest hazard score is {level} or more, the at-risk level your organisation states. Each figure adds up the value of those assets, today and in 2030, 2050 and 2100 under the chosen climate scenario. The range runs from the climate models' low projection to their high one. The movers are the assets whose score rises most by the last year, weighted by their value.
detail.why: Only hazards scored for the likelihood or strength of damaging conditions count. Live readings of today's conditions, crop-only scales and ground-susceptibility classes are context and never count.

detail.what: By {year}, the value of assets that newly reach your at-risk level is {share}% of the book or more, the materiality your organisation states. It is the first year this happens under the chosen scenario.
In no year up to 2100 does the value of assets newly reaching your at-risk level come to {share}% of the book, the materiality your organisation states.

portfolio.expected_loss.basis.label: Expected loss on your stated method

detail.what: For each loan: the outstanding balance × your stated yearly chance of a damaging event × your stated damage ratio, for the loan's main hazard at its score band. The lifetime figure adds this up year by year until the loan matures, using the maturity on your loan tape.
detail.why: It is the expected loss of collateral value, not a credit loss under Basel or IFRS 9: it has no probability of default and is not discounted.

detail.what: These loans have no maturity on the loan tape, so they have no lifetime expected loss, and the book's lifetime total is not shown.
detail.next: Add each loan's remaining maturity to the loan tape and import it again.

portfolio.concentration.basis.label: Value at risk by region and hazard

detail.what: Each holding's climate value at risk (its value less its climate-adjusted value) is added up by region and by the hazard that leads its score. A common-shock cluster is the holdings that share one leading hazard in one region: a single event would hit them together.
detail.why: The effective number of regions is how many equal, independent bets the book behaves like: one divided by the sum of each region's squared share of value. Hazards are counted the same way. Clusters follow from shared hazard and place; no correlation model is fitted. Holdings not yet scored are counted in the coverage and never treated as safe.

detail.what: One region holds more than {limit}% of the book's value, so one regional event reaches a large part of it.
One hazard leads the score of more than {limit}% of the scored value, so the book's climate risk depends heavily on it.
The book behaves like fewer than {limit} equal, independent regional bets, so one regional event moves much of it.

portfolio.stranding.collateral.label: Your brown discount by energy grade

detail.what: Your stated brown discount for each energy-performance (EPC) grade lowers the value of the property securing each real-estate loan. That raises the loan-to-value ratio. Any part of a loan the lowered collateral no longer covers is shown as exposure uncovered.
detail.why: Loans without an EPC grade, a collateral value or an outstanding balance are counted as not assessed. They are never given a figure.

portfolio.stranding.energy.label: Your brown discount and retrofit cost by grade

detail.what: Your stated brown discount for each energy-performance (EPC) grade gives each property's value at risk. Your stated retrofit cost for the grade gives the spend that removes the risk.
detail.why: Properties without an EPC grade or a value are counted as not assessed. They are never given a figure.

portfolio.catastrophe.basis.label: Shared events across each hazard and region

detail.what: A simulation of many years of events. Each event strikes one hazard in one region at that zone's yearly rate, and every insured location in the zone takes its loss from the same event. Each location's expected loss stays as your stated damage ratios and event chances set it.
detail.why: Locations in one zone move together; different zones are independent. This is how the simulation defines dependence. It is not a fitted vendor catastrophe model, nor an approved internal model.

detail.what: The probable maximum loss is read at a return period your organisation chooses, and none is set.
detail.next: Set the return period in your calculation settings.

detail.what: Net is the gross loss after ceding, event by event: the quota share takes its part of every loss, and the catastrophe excess-of-loss layer recovers on each zone event, in the yearly total and in the largest event.
detail.why: Reinstatements are taken as unlimited. Their premiums, and any aggregate treaty, are not modelled.

portfolio.combined_var.basis.label: Physical and transition in one simulation

detail.what: One simulation per holding over both drivers, on the stated method. Physical: its climate discount, varied across its score's confidence interval or the stated uncertainty. Transition: the stated stranded share for its sector, scenario and year, varied within the stated uncertainty. The two are combined {dependence}.
detail.why: Each holding can lose at most its value once.

portfolio.combined_var.no_dependence.label: Needs how physical and transition risks combine

detail.what: The combined figure needs your organisation's choice of how a holding's physical and transition losses combine, and none is set.
detail.next: Choose it in your calculation settings.

portfolio.transition.basis.label: Your carbon price and stranded share by sector

detail.what: For each loan, the transition expected loss is the outstanding balance × your stated stranded share for the borrower's sector under the scenario and year. The transition score is the larger of two: the carbon cost at your stated carbon price as a share of revenue, and that stranded share.
detail.why: Financed emissions here are the borrower's gross scope 1 and 2 emissions, as reported or, where none are reported, estimated from sector averages (EXIOBASE) and marked as estimated. The figure attributed to your loans (PCAF) is on the risk indicators page.

portfolio.resilience.basis.label: Your adaptation effectiveness and retrofit cost

detail.what: Each property's physical loss is its value × your discount for physical risk. The loss avoided is that loss × your stated adaptation effectiveness for the hazard. The spend is the value × your stated retrofit cost share for the hazard's score band.
detail.why: Whether the spend counts as EU Taxonomy climate-adaptation capex is decided by the Taxonomy's own criteria, not here.

portfolio.value_loss.basis.label: Your haircut across each score's range

detail.what: Each asset's stated valuation haircut is read at its score's band, and at the bands of the low and high ends of the score's confidence interval. The figure and its range add these up across the book.
detail.why: An analyst override is carried as it stands, without a range. An asset whose score has no confidence interval adds the same amount to both ends.

dependence.additive: by adding them, up to the holding's whole value
dependence.max: by taking the larger of the two
